content: The grey literature review emphasized the critical importance of understanding how individuals access health information. Without this knowledge, even the most well-crafted health messages may fail to reach their intended audience if they are disseminated through channels that are not visible or accessible to the target population. Media consumption patterns vary significantly across different groups, and it is essential to assess these variations to ensure effective communication. Additionally, the credibility and trustworthiness of the information source play a pivotal role in influencing behavioral changes. Few studies have explored the use of social media during the preparation and recovery phases of health emergencies. This represents a gap in the literature that warrants further investigation. The Internal Steering Group (ISG), established in 2014, consists of WHO staff involved in emergency preparedness, response, and communications. The ISG held an initial informal discussion in October 2014, followed by a formal meeting in March 2015. The group has been responsible for overseeing the scoping of the guidelines, selecting members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), managing systematic reviews, and producing the final guidelines. A complete list of ISG members is available in Annex 1, Table 6.3. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was formed through consultations with key partners, stakeholders, and the ISG to identify experts in areas such as emergencies, pandemics, disaster risk management, communications, anthropology, sociology, and health systems. Gender and regional balance were also considered in the selection process. Annex 1, Table 7 provides a full list of GDG members, their affiliations, expertise, and declared interests. The initial GDG chairperson, Marsha Vanderford, was the Associate Director for Communications at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, Georgia, USA. She chaired the GDG during the scoping meeting, question formulation, and evidence search phases. However, in January 2016, Dr. Vanderford joined WHO staff and was no longer eligible to serve on the GDG. She was replaced by two co-chairpersons: Amrita Gill Bailey from Johns Hopkins University, USA, and Peter Banga from the Polytechnic School of Journalism and Media Studies, Zimbabwe. They co-chaired the guideline development meeting in Geneva in February 2017, where the GDG used retrieved evidence to make recommendations. The External Review Group (ERG) included risk communication experts and practitioners with experience in emergencies, academic research on risk communication strategies, and work in regions prone to outbreaks and emergencies. Their role was to review the draft guidelines for clarity, assess the practicality and usefulness of the recommendations, and identify contextual issues, implementation implications, and other relevant concerns. Annex 1, Table 8 lists ERG members, their affiliations, and any declared conflicts of interest. To manage conflicts of interest, all experts involved in the guideline development process, including GDG and ERG members, systematic reviewers, methodologists, and consultants, were required to complete a Declaration of Interest (DOI) form. The secretariat conducted online searches of potential members' activities and publications to identify any competing interests. Short biographies of GDG members were posted publicly for comments before their membership was confirmed. The secretariat reviewed all declared interests before each meeting to determine if any participants had conflicts that could preclude or limit their participation. Any potentially competing interests were referred to the WHO Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics Office for review. Participants were also asked to update their DOI forms before each meeting, and these were summarized and presented to the group for transparency. The dissemination and evaluation of the guidelines are critical to their success. Effective packaging, targeting, marketing, and dissemination strategies are essential to reach decision-makers and practitioners responsible for risk communication during health emergencies. The guidelines will be translated into all UN official languages and local languages in high-risk regions. They will be marketed through policy briefs, emails to operational partners, schools of journalism, and networks of community radio stations. The guidelines will also be shared on the WHO website, distributed to relevant stakeholders, and promoted at academic conferences and training sessions. Monitoring the use of the guidelines will involve direct feedback from users, online surveys, tracking references in related publications, and feedback from OpenWHO course participants. The guidelines will also be evaluated during Joint External Evaluations (JEEs) of Member States' core capacities for managing public health emergencies. A review and update of the guidelines are planned five years after publication, or sooner if new evidence necessitates changes in recommended practices.
